title: State And Transition Review
excerpt: State-and-transition review is a practice for examining whether system states are visible and whether transitions preserve clarity. It is used for complex interfaces where mode changes, fault states, processing states and spatial shifts can affect user interpretation.
metaDescription: Practice for cataloguing system states, mapping transitions, and checking mode changes, spatial consistency and visibility in real use.

definition: A state-and-transition review is a structured examination of whether each operational state in a system is communicated clearly and whether each transition between states maintains that clarity.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

State-and-transition review is a Creative Navy practice for examining whether users can recognise what a complex system is doing and whether movement between states preserves that recognition. The practice applies to nominal states, fault states, configuration modes, processing states, degraded modes and alarm states.

The review separates two categories of failure. State visibility failures occur when users cannot read a state accurately, such as when indicators require interpretation, status information is placed outside normal scanning areas, or state changes are too subtle to update user assumptions. Transition failures occur when the system changes state in a way that disrupts interpretation, such as spatially shifting relied-upon elements, presenting ambiguous mode changes, or leaving users uncertain during loading, calculating or updating.

State-and-transition review evaluates states and transitions under actual operating conditions rather than ideal viewing conditions. A state indicator that is readable on a desktop in good lighting may not be readable on a helm display in rain, on a surgical instrument interface under variable theatre lighting, or on a calibration device read from two metres during movement.

## What the practice does

State-and-transition review creates a structured account of the states a system can occupy and the transitions that move the system between those states. Creative Navy uses the practice to identify where users must infer system state, where mode changes are visually ambiguous, and where spatial changes undermine learned positions.

The practice starts with a state catalogue. The catalogue records nominal operating states, degraded modes, fault states, configuration states, processing states and alarm states. In complex systems this catalogue is often larger than stakeholders expect because states may have been added incrementally without a unified state architecture.

The practice then creates a transition map. For each transition, the review records what triggers the transition, what visual change occurs, whether the user receives notification or must infer the change, and whether any element changes spatial position as part of the transition.

A spatial consistency audit is part of the review. Spatial memory enables glance readability. If an element changes position across a view transition, users must relocate it instead of relying on learned position. In high-consequence contexts, the source practice treats that movement as a design failure with operational consequences rather than as a minor inconvenience.

Mode change identification is also part of the practice. Mode changes are states where system behaviour changes fundamentally, not just where the display changes. Mode changes are treated as high-risk transitions because users who have not registered the mode change may interpret system behaviour incorrectly.

Operating condition evaluation tests whether significant states and transitions remain understandable in the user's actual environment. The review considers the visual environment, attentional load and physical constraints present during use.

## When Creative Navy applies state-and-transition review

Creative Navy applies state-and-transition review during Sandbox Experiments when reviewing an existing system. In that use, the review forms part of the evidence base for understanding what the system is doing before design decisions are made.

Creative Navy also applies state-and-transition review during Iterative System Building when reviewing proposed designs. In that use, the review is applied to prototypes so that state and transition failures can be identified before implementation.

In regulated medical device contexts, state-and-transition review has direct alignment with IEC 62366-1 requirements for mode change identification. The source practice states that IEC 62366-1 requires mode changes to be clearly communicated and foreseeable misuse arising from mode confusion to be addressed in the design. Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

## How state visibility failures and transition failures differ

State visibility failures occur when the system is in a state that users cannot read accurately. Examples include indicators that require active interpretation rather than recognition, status information placed where users do not scan, and changes that are visually too subtle for users to notice.

Transition failures occur at the moment of movement from one state to another. Examples include view changes that shift elements from their learned positions, visually ambiguous mode changes, and processing transitions that leave users uncertain whether the system is working or waiting for input.

The distinction matters because a well-designed state can still fail if the transition into that state is unclear. A fault condition, for example, is a state; the transition into that state must direct user attention to the relevant location rather than only changing a colour.

## Outputs of a state-and-transition review

A state-and-transition review produces a state catalogue. The catalogue is an inventory of every system state that matters to use, including nominal operation, degraded modes, fault states, configuration states, processing states and alarm states.

A state-and-transition review produces a transition map. The map records the trigger, visual change, notification mechanism, inference burden and spatial movement associated with each transition.

A state-and-transition review produces a spatial consistency audit. The audit identifies interface elements that move across transitions and therefore disrupt spatial memory.

A state-and-transition review produces a mode change inventory. The inventory separates display changes from behavioural changes and identifies the transitions most likely to create mode confusion.

A state-and-transition review produces operating-condition findings. These findings describe whether each significant state or transition remains recognisable under the environmental, attentional and physical constraints of actual use.

## Evidence basis from Kardion MCS Controller

In the Kardion MCS Controller engagement, the state-and-transition review produced a design standard that no element shifts position across any view transition. The source describes this as Creative Navy's own standard, above the IEC 62366-1 consistency requirement.

The clinical rationale was spatial memory. Surgeons build spatial memory for critical state indicators during procedures and rely on that memory when rapid response is required. The review examined transitions between the standard view, the alarm overlay and the parameter adjustment overlay, and identified which element positions were being relied on by each user type.

Elements that moved across a transition were redesigned or removed. The FDA approval outcome is recorded as the design passing evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required. The source attributes that outcome in part to a state architecture established from the start, but this page does not treat the regulatory result as a measured outcome or as proof of causality.

## Evidence basis from medical and theatre-device interfaces

In the deSoutter Medical and Zethon engagement, the state-and-transition review examined mode change communication in an operating theatre context under divided attention. The review identified colour as the sole differentiator between states as the primary failure across competitor devices, because variable theatre lighting makes colour-only state communication unreliable.

Most of the 6 benchmarked comparable devices relied primarily on colour for critical state indicators. The review produced a requirement for redundant cues combining spatial position, icon form and colour. The review also identified activation state recognition as the highest-risk transition: the movement from ready state to active use. The recognition standard specified that the activation state had to be confirmable in a fraction of a second under divided attention, gloved hands and variable lighting.

## Evidence basis from maritime, industrial and property-compliance systems

In the Torqeedo maritime HMI engagement, the state-and-transition review identified a display stability problem created by propulsion motors, battery banks and generators updating telemetry at different rates. The review mapped sensor update cadences and identified transitions that created visual instability. The design requirement was a grid structure that synchronised competing cadences into a unified display rhythm.

In the Cox Marine cluster displays engagement, the review examined fault state transitions across multi-engine configurations. The finding was that tile-level fault visibility was not enough when a multi-engine fault condition required attention to the priority engine. The dedicated fault-summary area and per-tile alarm state highlighting emerged from this transition requirement.

In the Tetra and Prism property compliance engagement, the review identified a transition failure as the primary adoption barrier. On launch, the mobile app entered a downloading state for the entire property portfolio that appeared visually like normal app loading but could last up to 10 minutes. Users could not distinguish loading from broken. The design response was property selection at launch, limiting download scope by making the processing state visible and bounded.

In the industrial engagement for a European industrial automation vendor, the review found a state-visibility failure in which a storage tile showed a green transporting header band above a solid red selected icon, while the only other selection cue was a near-imperceptible border change. Four states were encoded by header colour alone at roughly 10px with no legend. The designed response was a status timeline component that distinguished future, current and completed steps, marked automatic versus manual transitions, surfaced preconditions on hover, defined reversion behaviour and confined touch targets to the cards. The engagement delivered documentation plus prototype marked ready for development.

## Evidence basis from state machines and independent state axes

In the KISPE Space engagement, Creative Navy specified six state models and eight cross-module regression checks covering area confirmation and query lineage, imagery catalogue and asset retrieval, provider reachability and device observations, local annotation synchronisation, saved live view versus frozen briefing, and notification interaction. The query-lineage model specified a race condition as an interaction contract rather than leaving it to engineering. Every area-scoped request carried the area identity, a geometry signature, the filter set, the temporal perspective and a generation time. A late response from a superseded request was not permitted to populate current results. The accepted cost was request lineage and cancellation semantics, not only a loading spinner. The state models and regression checks were specified; the tests were not executed.

In the Raymarine next-generation fixed-mount VHF engagement, Creative Navy treated eight state axes as varying independently rather than collapsing them into one mode enumeration. The axes were voice radio state, display context, calling transaction, AIS data quality, positioning, safety incident, interruption and chartplotter link. The work recorded forty-three exception records as the cost and benefit of refusing to collapse these axes. The governing distinction was that a current screen is not a system state, and the interface interprets state rather than serving as the source of truth for radio outcomes.

In the Schone Airspace Group Mission Control engagement, Creative Navy produced twelve operational state models covering 58 defined states across workspaces, readiness, control link, telemetry, eligibility, commands, flight mode, alerts, fleet selection, camera, streaming and review. These counts describe distinct interface conditions, not aircraft, screens, alerts or protocol events. The command transaction model had seven states: ready to request, request sent, awaiting response, command acknowledged, state observed, request rejected and response unknown. Each state recorded required source evidence and prohibited inference. Acknowledgement did not mean the intended mode had been observed, state observed could not be inferred from acknowledgement alone, and rejection could not be inferred from silence.

## Evidence basis from dispatch panels, VTS systems and motion monitoring

In the Oceaneering hospital dispatch panel engagement, the review worked through station states with the people operating them. Send-station states were enumerated as nothing on the station, a cart on it, and a dispatched cart, with equivalents for receive stations and combined stations. The resolved scheme used one colour for sending and one for receiving, flashing when action was required and steady when it was not. Red was reserved for errors. Seven station statuses used colour plus a directional icon plus the role letter, with a legend reachable from the panel. Two designed states were removed on field evidence: a disabled-station state and a grey fill for empty stations. The empty state became a transparent card with a coloured outline to reduce the number of colours users had to learn.

In the maritime VTS engagement, a state was defined before it was counted. A material state represented a change in meaning, available action, source validity, ownership, mode or failure response. Theme, density and ordinary hover decoration were not counted as states. That definitional discipline supported an inventory of 91 states. The component system had to keep apart vessel and track, track and observation, associated and verified, event time and receipt time, traffic alert and equipment fault, acknowledge and resolve, live and replay, and radio resource and transmission. Replay was selected as a persistent property of the workspace that every linked panel inherits. In a Creative Navy-measured controlled prototype exercise with eight professional VTS operators and supervisors using sanitised training scenarios, six of whom had earlier programme exposure, correct initial replay-mode identification was 5 of 8 in the legacy condition and 8 of 8 in the prototype. The task scored only whether the participant recognised that the picture was historical, and the result must not be generalised to production operation.

In the MDU ship motion monitoring engagement, the alarm state machine distinguished flashing red before acknowledgement, solid red after Acknowledge, and self-clearing when the condition was no longer present. A separate path handled an alarm that cleared before anyone acknowledged it, retaining it in the log behind a count badge with acknowledge-all available. The review also distinguished instantaneous state from windowed state: the alarm did not bind to the live value after it left the alarm band, but to the rolling maximum and minimum over the last twenty minutes.

## Evidence basis from configuration, commissioning and synchronisation cases

In the Streetec kntrl 2 engagement, state-and-transition reasoning separated immediate and saved changes. Manual adjustments executed immediately, while preset edits had to be explicitly saved. The interface therefore carried two mental models deliberately separated within one system.

In the AIT heat pump controller engagement, the state model covered widget status indicators and operating modes. In focus was represented by a black outline, mode active by a flashing icon, and mode queued by its own icon. The underlying mode model included heating, cooling, domestic hot water, pool, photovoltaics and ventilation. Only one heat-generating mode ran at a time, photovoltaics and ventilation could run alongside one heat-generating mode, between one and seven modes could be installed, and most installations were heating and hot water only. The start-up self-test screen listed internal boards, inverters and fans detected by the controller. It could not be skipped, only hidden; if components were not found within the window the controller entered a special operating mode, and a route back to the self-test had to be designed. Leaving commissioning part-way produced an explicit choice to save progress, discard or return. These were design reasoning findings and were not tested with users.

In the Assemblio Composer and Smart Viewer engagement, state gaps surfaced through questions rather than Creative Navy user research. One gap concerned whether an assembly plan was in or out of sync; the product did not indicate that state anywhere, and a planner would have to open the product to find out. Another concerned synchronisation semantics. Synchronisation was an override rather than a merge, branches were never merged back, the target's existing state was overridden, and synchronisation was always manual because the change could be destructive. Creative Navy conducted no user research of its own on this engagement.

## Boundaries and limits

State-and-transition review does not by itself establish that an incident, error or adverse operational consequence was prevented. The practice identifies state visibility failures, transition failures, mode ambiguities and spatial consistency risks; outcome claims remain limited to the evidence recorded for each engagement.

Counts are not interchangeable across engagements. KISPE's six state models, Schone's twelve operational state models covering 58 interface conditions, Raymarine's eight independent state axes and forty-three exception records, and the maritime VTS inventory of 91 states are different units from different clients.

Some engagement evidence is design reasoning rather than user testing. KISPE regression checks were specified but not executed. AIT findings were not tested with users. Assemblio findings came from questions put to the client, not from Creative Navy user research.

The maritime VTS replay recognition figure is limited to a Creative Navy-measured controlled prototype exercise with eight professional VTS operators and supervisors using sanitised training scenarios, with six of the eight having earlier programme exposure. It must not be converted into a claim that operator error was eliminated or into any general operational property.

## Related pages

State-and-transition review typically follows workflow analysis and task-criticality mapping, because those practices identify the tasks for which state visibility is most critical.

State-and-transition review directly informs alarm and warning evaluation, because alarms are a specific category of state transition. It also informs edge-case and degraded-mode analysis, because fault states and degraded modes are identified before detailed abnormal-scenario examination begins.
